newsitem.title: USA: Dlr surges on Greenspan, ends sharply higher in US.
newsitem.headline: Dlr surges on Greenspan, ends sharply higher in US.

text.p: The dollar ended broadly higher on Thursday after Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan gave his clearest warning yet that interest rates might be raised for the first time in almost two years.

The strong gains easily wiped out earlier losses that came in the wake of a report showing that the U.S. trade deficit widened to its highest level in nearly a decade. The rally's momentum was also helped by a short squeeze, analysts said.
The dollar climbed against the mark to settle at 1.6925/35, near its session high of 1.6940, compared to the opening at 1.6725/35.
Against the yen, the greenback easily sailed through the 123-level to close at 123.70/75 also near session highs of 123.77, against an opening at 122.62/67.

Testifying before a joint committee of Congress, Greenspan said the economy has "a great deal a vigor" and said strength in the job market could lead to higher inflation. He said the central bank must look beyond the current rosy economic data when setting monetary policy because the effects of any changes in rates might not be felt for a year or more.
Some analysts read his comments as a strong hint that the Fed could tighten short-term interest rates when the central bank's policy committee meets on Tuesday.
"He raised the possibility of a Fed tightening ... and that helped underpin the dollar," said Rick Gomes, foreign exchange manager at Republic National Bank of New York.

The dollar had tumbled at the opening after the Commerce Department reported the January U.S. trade gap shot up 21.1 percent to a larger-than-expected $12.71 billion. But strong demand after the Fed chief's comments wiped out the losses.
"The dollar had been weaker ... from the trade data. But when Greenspan started commenting, it went off to the races," said Bob Near, vice president at the Bank of New York.

The deficit also raised some fears of trade frictions in the market. The U.S. deficit with Japan edged up 0.7 percent to $4.29 bilion in January while the politically sensitive trade gap with China surged by 40.8 percent to $3.72 billion.

Dealers said a short-squeeze added to the gains after Greenspan's comments as market players who had bet on further weakness in the dollar during its morning retreat had to buy the U.S. currency back at higher levels.
"People had gone short this morning, especially dollar/Swiss," said Near.

Gomes also noted that the dollar was helped by a relatively stable reaction in stocks and bonds to Greenspan's testimony. Although the yield on the long bond moved above 7.0 percent briefly, it soon settled back with the 30-year U.S. Treasury bond closing up 11/32 to yield 6.96 percent.
The Dow Industrials closed off over 50 points to 6820.
There was no overnight trading in Tokyo due to the Vernal Equinox public holiday in Japan.
The British pound weakened against the dollar, slipping to $1.5935/45 at the close from $1.5963/73.
The dollar moved higher against the Swiss franc to 1.4530/40 against it opening at 1.4350/57. It settled at Canadian $1.3791/96 compared to C$1.3745/50.
The dollar closed at 0.7860/65 Australian dollars compared to $0.7881/86 at the open.
